column4: This describes believers being struck by adversity and shaken until they ask when God's help will come, then answers that God's help is near. It is a concrete communal scene of hardship with relief promised within it.

The section links ease to the Quran being made accessible for remembrance; this ayah says hearts find rest through remembrance of God (بِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ تَطْمَئِنُّ الْقُلُوبُ). It develops what remembrance can bring beyond access to recitation.

In the counsel about responding to needy relatives, this warns against keeping a hand bound to the neck or extending it without limit. The section joins ease shown to others with the giver's path and the miser's opposite path; this ayah places giving and withholding in a concrete hand image.

The helpers prefer the emigrants over themselves even in privation (خَصَاصَةٌ) and are praised for being protected from miserliness (شُحَّ نَفْسِهِ). This is a specific charitable response under hardship, set against the miserly path in 92:10.

In the campaign context, the weak, sick, and those without means to contribute are excused from blame. This is a specific easing of a difficult obligation in the same surah that later recalls the hour of hardship.

This gives the blind, lame, and sick exemption from blame in the campaign setting. It repeats the concrete pattern of accommodation for illness and bodily limitation that the section invokes through the fasting concession.

After the preceding command to fight, this says God has lightened the burden (خَفَّفَ عَنكُمْ), knowing the believers' weakness. It is a specific easing of a strenuous duty and echoes the section's secondary sense of ease as lightness.
Job calls on God when harm has touched him, appealing to God's mercy. This gives the section's hardship-and-ease image another prophet's specific plea from within affliction.
God answers Job and removes the harm that had touched him. This is the distinct relief in the scene begun in 21:83, paralleling the section's claim that trial is met by easing.

This recalls Dhun-Nun's appeal from the darkness after he departed in anger, when he thought God would not constrain him. It is another prophet's specific plea from distress, alongside the section's examples of Moses asking for his affair to be made easy.
God answers Jonah, rescues him from anguish, and says He likewise rescues the believers. This ayah contributes the deliverance that follows the distress in 21:87.

This describes good fortune coming after affliction (نَعْمَاءَ بَعْدَ ضَرَّاءَ) and the person's claim that hardship has gone. It offers a specific sequential framing of relief, illuminating the section's emphasis on ease accompanying hardship.
